svg.title: A nurse is caring for a client with a subclavian central line. Which actions reduce the client's risk of a central line-associated bloodstream infection? Select all that apply.
svg.desc: Scrub the hub 15 seconds with friction, change the transparent dressing every 7 days (gauze every 2 days, either one sooner if damp, loose or soiled), and pull the line the day it stops being needed — that last one prevents more infections than any technique. Why 2 minutes is wrong here: the chlorhexidine–alcohol prep has two times, and the site decides which one. Dry site (chest, arm, abdomen — so a subclavian line) = 30 seconds of back-and-forth friction. Moist site (groin, axilla — a femoral line) = 2 minutes . Either way, let it dry completely ; the drying is what kills, not the wiping. This client has a subclavian line, so 30 seconds. Drawing blood from the line does not itself cause CLABSI — poor technique at the hub does. And femoral is the highest -infection site, not a request you would make.
